prompt:
Extract a SysML v2 model from the document as a list of facts. Each fact has unit_id (the sentence it comes from), type and slots. Give only the slots that have a value, as a list of {slot, value} pairs; for composition give one 'parts' pair per part.

Types and slots:
  attribute(owner,name,value,unit) action(performer,label) state(owner,label) constraint(subject,expression) requirement(subject,text)
  composition(whole,parts) flow(source,target,payload) succession(before,after) transition(from,to,trigger) allocation(action,to)

Name each element by its full name as first introduced in the document.
RULES:
- Resolve every entity-valued slot using all the text you are given. If a sentence refers to an element by an alias, abbreviation, pronoun or shorter description, write the element's full name as first introduced. If a sentence says an element receives or uses an item and the text you are given states which element produces or sends that item, emit a flow from that producer to the receiver. If an element cannot be determined from the text you are given, use null; never guess.
- Never write placeholder words such as "any", "all", "some state" for an unstated element; use null.
- Do not merge differently named things unless the text says they are the same.
- Emit one action for EVERY behavior verb phrase, including passive voice (performer null), capability statements, displays, logs, generates and reports. label = the verbatim verb phrase with its object.
- Emit a requirement for every NORMATIVE statement (shall, must, should, will, is required to, needs to). Purpose, goal or benefit sentences are not requirements.
- Emit a state for every named mode or state; transitions use the state names, with from null when the prior state is not stated.
- Emit a succession only for an EXPLICIT temporal connective between two actions ("then", "after", "once", "before", "when ... is complete", "next", "finally"); before/after are the action labels. Never use succession for cause or data transfer.
- Resolve a pronoun or "this/these" performer to the element named in the preceding sentence and write that element's name; if it cannot be resolved, use null. Never output a pronoun as a slot value.
- Drop determiners and quantifiers from element names ("Each Soil Moisture Probe" -> "Soil Moisture Probe", "the system" -> "system").
- allocation.to must be a component or actor, never a mode or state.
- Emit a constraint for every threshold, limit, period or deadline stated with a number; expression = the verbatim phrase.
- Emit a flow for every sentence in which an element sends, transmits, reports, displays, commands or delivers an item (target null if the receiver is not named).
 Also list under "entities" every system element, actor or item named in the document units, with its full name and any alias the text explicitly declares for it (e.g. 'hereafter X', 'known as X', 'called X'); aliases [] if none. Return JSON {"entities": [...], "facts": [...]}.

Document units:
U0027: MBT is one specific interpretation of the high-level TBO vision, and is the starting point from which specific challenges can be identified and studied, contributing to the refinement of the MBT concept and the overall body of knowledge related to TBO. 1.1 NAS Shortfalls Addressed by MBT This section summarizes the shortfalls in the current NAS that are addressed by MBT, as shown in Table 1.
U0028: These shortfalls are consistent with those identified in the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) TBO Concept Document [1].
U0029: The ICAO TBO Concept Document provides high-level guidance for resolving these shortfalls, and the MBT concept provides a specific vision for resolving the shortfalls that is consistent with the ICAO TBO Concept.
U0030: Table 1.
U0031: NAS Shortfalls Addressed by MBT Shortfalls MBT Improvements Data exchanged between airspace users and the FAA are too sparse to support accurate trajectory prediction across all phases of flight and trajectory synchronization across automation systems.
U0032: The data needed by all relevant airspace users, aircraft, and FAA automation systems to develop accurate, consistent 4DT predictions are available to all relevant systems.
U0033: The use of open trajectories, including tactical maneuvers, causes poor trajectory predictability.
U0034: Aircraft operate on closed trajectories to the extent possible, which improves trajectory predictability.
U0035: Insufficient publication of trajectory changes and lack of trajectory synchronization result in poor trajectory predictability.
U0036: Publication of all trajectory changes and advanced exchange of trajectory information between ground automation systems and the aircraft allow for trajectory synchronization across systems, resulting in consistent trajectory predictions across systems.
U0037: Poor trajectory predictability inhibits strategic (longer look ahead) trajectory management.
U0038: Improved trajectory predictability, improved coordination capabilities, and use of 4DTs enable controllers to use strategic, closed clearances.
U0039: A high level of trajectory predictability becomes the new norm.
U0040: Enhanced predictability will improve TFM performance and provide a more consistent flow of air traffic, where demand will more accurately meet available capacity, reducing or eliminating delay.
U0041: All applicable NAS constraints, both dynamic (e.g., TFM) and static (e.g., crossing restrictions) are published such that they can be known by all airspace users and relevant automation systems.
U0042: All constraints affecting a given aircraft are reflected in the 4DT.
U0043: Lack of knowledge about certain types of constraints prevents airspace users from planning business-efficient, acceptable trajectories.
U0044: Those constraints also are unknown to every ground automation system, causing aircraft to be handled with an open- ended clearance when the constraints are encountered.
U0045: Insufficient mechanisms to allow traffic managers and controllers to efficiently and effectively amend flights’ routes cause route amendment backlogs during disruptive NAS events.
U0046: Traffic managers apply constraints to efficiently amend trajectories as NAS events evolve, enabling a more flexible and responsive ATM system that can take full advantage of available airspace and drastically reduce delay.2 There is not a good mechanism that allows controllers and traffic managers to predict the downstream consequences of an action or decision on specific aircrafts’ trajectories.
U0047: Downstream effects of actions on a trajectory are considered in decision making associated with a given trajectory, including tactical control actions.
U0048: By quantifying time-based performance as a metric that complements existing PBN metrics, all IFR aircraft may be managed by a single ATM concept that maximizes efficiency while maintaining an acceptable level of safety risk.
U0049: Current time of arrival control (TOAC) standards establish a minimum performance requirement that some aircraft will be certified for while others will not.
U0050: This type of standard may inadvertently introduce unacceptable safety risk into the NAS and creates a mixed equipage environment in which one ATM concept applies to those who meet the standard while another concept must be applied to those who do not. 1.2 MBT Overview The MBT concept can be summarized by the following key points.  MBT applies to all aircraft operating according to Instrument Flight Rules (IFR).  Aircraft are assigned 4DTs, which are negotiated, closed trajectories, from their current state to their destination.  A NAS Constraint Service publishes common information about NAS constraints to all stakeholders.  Trajectory constraints can be mapped to NAS constraints to facilitate identifying affected aircraft when NAS constraints change.  All aircraft follow their negotiated, assigned trajectories, complying with trajectory constraints.  Trajectory constraints and associated tolerances are defined based on the flight’s individual performance capabilities and the situational need for the constraint. 2 This document does not describe the details of how traffic managers or traffic management automation determines what trajectory constraints to impose on each flight.
